newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-ANTITRUST BILL NAMED FOR CURT FLOOD.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-ANTITRUST BILL NAMED FOR CURT FLOOD.

text.p: A bill to partially lift Major League Baseball's antitrust exemption was introduced in the Senate Tuesday and named for former player Curt Flood, who died Monday of cancer in Los Angeles at age 59.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, who introduced the legislation, said he was honouring Flood because of Flood's 1970 law suit against baseball's reserve clause that tied players to teams.
Flood lost the suit but it led to other action that eventually eliminated the reserve clause and let players move from team to team as free agents.

"The Curt Flood Act of 1997, named for the courageous player who challenged baseball's reserve clause, will benefit baseball fans because it will bring about sound reforms that ensure that baseball remains strong and is treated fairly and properly under the antitrust laws," Hatch, R-Utah, said.

The bill would eliminate baseball's antitrust exemption, granted in a 1922 Supreme Court decision, in labour negotiations and allow players and owners to file unfair labour complaints with the National Labour Relations Board.

Hatch first introduced the bill after a players' strike cancelled the 1994 World Series. The strike was ended in time for the 1995 season but a labour agreement with team owners was not reached until last December.

Flood was a star outfielder with the St. Louis Cardinals from 1958 to 1969 when he was traded to Philadelphia. He refused to go and filed a suit saying he should not be traded without his consent. After he lost, he played briefly with the Washington Senators in 1971 and then retired from baseball.
